title: Best Emergent Alternatives in 2026
summary: Emergent alternatives compared on what each plan bundles: hosting, a database and how it bills. Base44, Replit, Bolt.new, Lovable, Blink, v0 and more.
body_markdown:
Key takeaways:


- Six of the nine builders after ours include hosting and a database with no separate account, and four (Base44, Replit, Bolt.new and Lovable) do it on a free plan, Replit's for 30 days.
- Emergent's publishing docs charge each live web app 50 to 1,100 credits a month, $10 to $220 at its $0.20 top-up rate by our math.
- Blink is the closest match to Emergent's credit-priced hosting, while Lovable's docs say a live site uses no credits on its own.
- Emergent's GitHub export needs Standard or above, and secrets and database contents stay behind, so you move those by hand.


If you're comparing Emergent alternatives, you probably like the idea behind Emergent (emergent.sh): an AI app builder whose E-3 agent, launched in beta on the $200 Pro plan, drafts a phased plan, waits for your approval and builds the app end to end. What sends people looking is the bill: every prompt costs credits, and each published app pays a monthly hosting fee in credits.


So this list judges each builder on what its plan includes: hosting, a database and how both are charged. All prices were checked on November 13, 2026.


We put[Awesomic](https://www.awesomic.com/) first because it's our product. The other nine follow a rule you can check in vendor docs: builders that host the app and its database without a separate account and publish on a free plan, then those that need a paid plan to publish, then those covering one of the two, then neither. Within each group, the cheaper monthly plan goes first, then alphabetical order.


## What pushes builders off Emergent


Credit burn is the first complaint. Emergent's help center says a prompt can cost "from a handful of credits ... to hundreds", and large builds "hundreds or even thousands", but it lists only a few per-action rates, such as 5 to 20 credits per generated media asset.


In a[small r/indianstartups thread](https://www.reddit.com/r/indianstartups/comments/1qvjxzf/how_does_the_credit_utilization_works_in_emergent/) from February 2026, one builder said a single prompt burned 50 credits while the agent looped on its own error. It's one anecdotal Reddit report, and the docs let you cap credits per prompt in Settings → Billing.


Hosting is the second cost. Each published app pays a fixed monthly credit fee by tier (a mobile app adds 10), and Emergent warns that Starter "is not suitable for production apps under meaningful load".


Publishing tier Credits a month At $0.20 a credit (our math)


Starter 50 $10


Launch 125 $25


Grow 225 $45


Scale 450 $90


Elite 1,100 $220


Standard costs $20 a month, or $17 billed annually, for 100 credits, so one Launch-tier app outruns the plan before you've built anything.


A bigger plan doesn't make credits cheaper. By our math, Standard works out to $0.20 a credit billed monthly, a 250-credit top-up for $50 is also $0.20, and Pro's 750 credits for $200 come to about $0.27.


Plan limits are the third pressure: Free's 10 credits can't publish to production, and Terms §2.1 limits Free to "personal, non-commercial purposes". Lock-in, covered in the exit steps below, is the last, so each of the Emergent competitors that follow says how your code gets out.


## Emergent alternatives at a glance


Every builder here turns a prompt into a running app; the last column shows what the plan includes once it goes live.


Awesomic brings AI agents and vetted experts into one app. Start with a prompt to build a website, app, campaign, deck or video, then switch models or bring in a vetted expert without losing the project context. AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


Read the last two columns together: a free database is little use on a plan that can't publish to production, like Blink's and Emergent's free plans.


### 1. Awesomic


**Best for:** A cloud computer per project, four agents and an expert route


**Overview:** Awesomic gives you a cloud computer per project, with up to 1 TB of storage, where agents install, run and publish real programs, from a website to an internal CRM.


That machine keeps running unattended, and you can check progress from a browser, a desktop app or your phone. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or OpenCode build on models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI and others, all on one bill.


One click puts a working site on a live link, and on an expert plan you can hand a stalled task to a vetted expert from the same chat. More than 20,000 ideas have become delivered projects with us.


**Key features:**


- Agents working in parallel, one chat each, on the same project.
- A lead agent that can split a big build across several helper agents.
- GitHub as a connected app, and file downloads for 30 days after canceling.
- A team keychain: add an API key once and every teammate's agents can call it.


**Pricing:** Basic is $99 a person a month, and that $99 is the person's monthly AI budget; Light, Pro and Studio set it at $19, $199 and $499. Plans bill monthly and aren't refundable.


For current Awesomic plans and capabilities, see[the pricing page](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


Expert help is bought separately: the $3,219-a-month All-in-One plan covers design, copywriting, no-code development and QA, while a Dedicated expert, the plan for full-stack and mobile app development, is priced on a call.


**Pros:** Work continues with the laptop shut, a one-click live link, four agents on one bill, a vetted expert in the same chat on an expert plan


**Cons:** AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**How to start using it:**


1. Pick Basic, or an expert plan if you'll want a person on the work (an expert plan includes its own Light subscription).
2. Describe the app in a project and add its API keys to the team keychain.
3. Let one agent build while a second takes another part.
4. Publish to a live link and share the project with teammates.
5. Check spend per person and per model in the admin view.


**Why it's a good Emergent alternative:** You pick from four agents and several model makers on one bill, and on an expert plan a person can take over in the same chat when the agent loops. Ask us what limits apply to a live link before you move a production app.


**Final verdict:** Choose Awesomic when you want agents on their own cloud computer and will pay for an expert plan when a person must step in. For a database-backed app on a smaller budget, Lovable or Base44 include hosting and a database even on free plans.


To try it on Basic,[Get started](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


### 2. Base44


**Overview:** Base44, owned by Wix, builds "a managed backend, authentication, integrations, and hosting" into every plan, per its docs, so there's no second account to open.


The trade-off is two meters: message credits for building, from about 0.5 for a simple edit to 3 or 4 for an app-wide change, and integration credits for the services your running app calls.


**Key features:**


- Manual visual edits that cost no credits.
- Two-way GitHub sync from Builder, plus a source ZIP through its API.
- The Base44 CLI for local development.


**Pricing:** Free gives your personal workspace 5 message credits a day, capped at 25 a month, plus 100 integration credits. Starter runs $16 a month on yearly billing, or $20 monthly, and buys 100 message and 2,000 integration credits, while Builder is $40 billed yearly, or $50 monthly, for 250 and 10,000.


**Pros:** Hosting, database and auth on every plan, free visual edits, a ZIP route out


**Cons:** Two credit meters to track, GitHub sync only from Builder, unused credits expire each month


**Where it beats Emergent:** Hosting comes with the plan instead of a monthly fee per live app, and integrations draw on their own credits, so traffic doesn't eat build credits.


**Final verdict:** Choose Base44 for a database-backed app on a small budget, and watch the integration meter after launch.


### 3. Replit


**Overview:** Replit hosts the app and gives it a PostgreSQL-compatible database, both metered. Publishing draws on monthly credits first, then usage fees: Autoscale is $2 a month on its publishing-costs page, plus $0.60 per million compute units and $0.40 per million requests, and Reserved VMs start at $15 a month.


Development databases are free, while production ones are "billed for compute usage and storage". For unattended work, Core and Pro turn on Full build, which Replit says "allows Agent to work independently with more power and autonomy".


**Key features:**


- Background tasks, one active on Core and 10 on Pro.
- Two-way GitHub auto-sync and a "Download as zip" option.
- Database rollback of up to 28 days on Pro.


**Pricing:** Starter is free, with daily Agent credits, Lite build and one published app that "will automatically go down after 30 days" unless you re-publish it. Core is $20 a month, or $18 billed annually, for unlimited published apps and up to 5 builders, and Pro is $100, or $90 billed annually.


**Pros:** A free plan that publishes, Full build autonomy, ZIP and GitHub exits


**Cons:** Hosting cost grows with traffic, the free app expires after 30 days, Full build, connectors and Plan Mode need Core


**Pick it when:** You'd rather pay by usage for a quiet full-stack app, since Autoscale's $2 monthly base sits below Emergent's 50-credit Starter tier, $10 by our math.


**Final verdict:** Choose Replit to stay nearer the code, if a bill that tracks traffic is fine.


### 4. Bolt.new


**Overview:** Bolt.new, from StackBlitz, creates databases automatically ("Unlimited databases", per its docs) and hosts what you build on every plan.


The free tier has a hard edge: 10 GB of bandwidth and 333,333 requests a month, after which sites go offline until the reset. Pro raises that to 30 GB and 1M requests, then bills pay-as-you-go up to a cap you set.


**Key features:**


- Token metering, with paid tokens rolling over for two months while you subscribe.
- Supabase as an option on Pro and Teams.
- GitHub import and two-way sync, plus a project ZIP from the desktop site.


**Pricing:** The free plan includes 300K tokens daily and 1M a month. Pro is $25 billed monthly, or $18 a month on yearly billing, for 10M tokens, a custom domain and no daily cap.


**Pros:** Hosting and a database on Free, rollover tokens, an overage cap you control


**Cons:** Free sites go dark at the traffic cap, token use climbs as a project grows, hosting limits shared across projects


**Its edge over Emergent:** Pro keeps a site up past the included traffic on pay-as-you-go, to a cap you set, while Emergent's credit doc says a published app may be "taken down until you recharge" if the account is still negative after a low-credit renewal.


**Final verdict:** Choose Bolt.new for a fast first version on the free tier, and move to Pro before launch traffic arrives.


### 5. Lovable


**Overview:** Lovable's hosting docs are blunt: "Hosting is part of Lovable", publishing to a lovable.app address is free on every plan, and "A live site does not consume credits on its own." Usage-based Run credits still cover backend activity and AI features.


That backend is Lovable Cloud, built on Supabase's open-source foundation, with a database, auth, storage, realtime and functions. Lovable builds for the web only, though: its docs say it "does not generate React Native projects".


**Key features:**


- Git sync with GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket on every plan, into a new repo only.
- Unlimited workspace members on all plans.
- A code editor and code download from Pro.


**Pricing:** Free comes with 5 build credits daily, to a maximum of 30 monthly, alongside 20 Cloud credits. Pro starts at $25 a month, or $250 a year, for 100 credits, and Business starts at $50 monthly.


**Pros:** Hosting and a backend on the free plan, a free lovable.app address, monthly credit rollover on Pro and Business


**Cons:** Web only, no code editing or download on Free, traffic-heavy backends draw Run credits


**Why it's a good Emergent alternative:** Hosting comes with every plan, Free included, where Emergent charges each live app a monthly fee in credits.


**Final verdict:** Choose Lovable for a web app with a real backend that should stay live without a per-app hosting fee.


### 6. Anything


**Overview:** Anything is built around native mobile: it builds iOS and Android apps and handles App Store submission. Every project gets separate development and production PostgreSQL databases through Neon, and you publish to a created.app address, with a custom domain on Pro.


The catch is the entry point: its subscriptions doc says "Building an app requires a paid plan", though the Pro card's "Everything in Free, plus:" and a free-plan badge in its publish doc hint at a free tier.


**Key features:**


- Native mobile output for iPhone and Android, App Store submission included.
- Built-in auth, Stripe payments and file storage.
- Multi-agent runs and automated testing on Max.


**Pricing:** Pro 20k is $24 a month, or $19 billed annually, for 20,000 credits, and Max 200k is $239 monthly, or $199 annually, for 220,000 credits including a 10% bonus. Top-offs run from $12 for 10,000 credits to $240 for 200,000 and never expire.


**Pros:** Postgres included on paid plans, native mobile output, ZIP export from the Code tab


**Cons:** No free building plan, GitHub sync still "coming soon", monthly credits expire each cycle


**Why it made this list:** Unlike Emergent, it gives you a ZIP download, so the code can leave without a GitHub step.


**Final verdict:** Choose Anything for a phone app with a real database, and budget for a paid plan from the start.


### 7. Blink


**Overview:** Blink works the most like Emergent on hosting: production apps on a blinkpowered.com address pay credits by traffic tier, from 50 a month for 10K visits to 500 for 1M, with overage charged per 1,000 visits. Its docs add that "Overages never take your app offline."


A SQLite-compatible SQL database from Turso comes "at no extra cost" on every project, and preview URLs are free on all plans. Blink also documents a one-click import of Emergent code and FastAPI backends, though its guide covers Supabase data, not Emergent's MongoDB, so export your data separately.


**Key features:**


- Blink Claw, hosted agents that run 24/7 from Starter.
- Two-way GitHub sync, free on every plan per its docs.
- An AI gateway with 200+ models across text, image, video and speech, per its FAQ.


**Pricing:** Free gives you 5 daily credits, capped at 30 a month. Starter is $25 a month, or $13 billed annually, for 100 plan credits plus 5 a day, and Pro is $50, or $25 annually, for 200 credits.


**Pros:** A free database on every project, GitHub sync on Free per its docs (its pricing grid lists Git from Pro), free preview URLs


**Cons:** The 10K-visit tier uses half the Starter plan's 100 plan credits, code download costs 5 credits on Starter and Pro, production hosting and custom domains need Starter


**What it does better:** Its hosting tiers are set by visits, so a traffic forecast maps straight to a credit cost, and going over doesn't switch the app off.


**Final verdict:** Choose Blink if Emergent's model suits you but you want the hosting meter tied to visits.


### 8. Rocket.new


**Overview:** Rocket.new now sells itself as "Vibe Solutioning", with Build one of three capabilities beside Solve and Intelligence, all on one credit pool. Build still covers web apps, mobile, landing pages and SaaS, in Next.js or Flutter, with Android APKs.


On hosting, its credits doc says "There is no separate billing for compute, storage, or hosting", and every app gets a staging URL, with custom domains from Pro. The database is the catch: it connects through OAuth to your own Supabase account, with its own plan and bill.


**Key features:**


- A free "Fix it" for detected errors on paid plans.
- Unlimited team members.
- GitHub sync, two-way for Next.js TypeScript projects on Pro and up, push-only for other frameworks.


**Pricing:** Free gives you a one-time 20 credits with no card. Pro is $25 a month for 100 credits, Rocket is $50 for 250 and Booster is $250 for 1,500, and yearly billing saves 20%.


**Pros:** No separate hosting bill, free error fixes on paid plans, unlimited members


**Cons:** The database is a separate Supabase account and bill, two-way sync only for Next.js TypeScript, only 20 free credits ever


**Reason to shortlist it:** Fixing a detected error costs no credits on paid plans, which goes straight at the looping-fix complaint about Emergent.


**Final verdict:** Choose Rocket.new if you already run Supabase and want hosting without a separate bill.


### 9. Softgen


**Overview:** Softgen puts a managed Supabase database on both plans: "Basic Supabase (platform-managed)" on Starter, "Managed Supabase + backups" on Pro. Hosting sits outside the plan: its Academy docs say "hosting for production isn't directly included" and that it helps you set up free hosting on Vercel, and its deployment guide starts with a Vercel login.


Its public record is thin: the blog's last post dates from July 2025, the changelog's from March 2026, and the Academy docs still describe a $33-a-year membership the pricing page doesn't show.


**Key features:**


- Two AI models to build with on Starter, 12+ on Pro.
- GitHub export on every plan.
- Your own Supabase project as an option, added in February 2026.


**Pricing:** Starter is $25 a month for 500 credits and 10 projects, and Pro is $49 for 1,500 credits, unlimited projects, custom domains and one month of credit rollover. New accounts get free trial credits with no card.


**Pros:** A managed database from the entry plan, model choice on Pro, GitHub export on every plan


**Cons:** Hosting runs through Vercel, not the plan (its Academy docs point you to your own Vercel account), Academy docs out of step with the pricing page, extra project slots at $3 a year each


**The strongest argument:** Its $25 Starter pairs a managed Supabase database with GitHub export on the same plan.


**Final verdict:** Choose Softgen for a Supabase-backed prototype with a choice of models, and set up the Vercel side before launch.


### 10. v0


**Overview:** v0, from Vercel, bundles neither hosting nor a database. Apps deploy to your own Vercel project on a vercel.app address, and databases come from one-click Marketplace integrations such as Upstash, Neon, Supabase and Vercel Blob, each of which provisions a new user account on that service.


What you get back is front-end code in Next.js, React, Tailwind and shadcn, with a Git workflow built around branches and pull requests.


**Key features:**


- GitHub import with a branch and pull request workflow.
- Vercel preview deployments for each change.
- Rollover for unused monthly credits, which lapse after 65 days.


**Pricing:** Free gives you 7 messages a day, and new signups get $5 of one-time credits. Plus costs $30 per user monthly with $30 in credits per user and $2 of free credits per daily login, and Business is $100 per user a month.


**Pros:** Front-end code in a stack developers know, a real Git workflow, a free tier


**Cons:** You assemble the backend yourself, per-seat pricing, credits metered as dollars spent on tokens


**Where it fits:** When the interface matters most and a developer will run the hosting and data in accounts you control.


**Final verdict:** Choose v0 if you'd rather own every account behind the app than have a builder bundle them.


## What Emergent competitors charge to keep an app live


Build credits stop when you stop prompting, but hosting bills every month whether you touch the app or not. Emergent comes first as the baseline.


Of the builders that publish a hosting price, only Emergent and Blink set it as a fixed credit tier, so each extra live app or traffic step comes out of the pool you build with; Replit also draws publishing from monthly credits, by usage.


Base44, Lovable, Bolt.new, Rocket.new and paid Anything plans charge no separate hosting fee. Base44 draws credits only for the services your app calls, so before you settle on it, weigh its two meters against our list of[Base44 alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/base44-alternatives) .


## How much each builder does without you


Emergent's E-3 agent is the baseline for hands-off building: it produces a phased plan you approve, then runs end to end, with a Mission Control view to pause or redirect it and Auto-HITL answering the agent's own questions. Its docs cap a run at 10,000 tool calls per message and 4 hours of wall-clock time.


Most alternatives document autonomy less precisely, naming a mode or plan rather than a cap: Replit's Full build on Core and Pro, or multi-agent runs on Anything's Max.


What no cap settles is who fixes the app when the agent can't. In an[r/nocode thread from March 2026](https://www.reddit.com/r/nocode/comments/1rxvkvc/) , the top reply said that when a full-app builder breaks, "you're either reverse-engineering generated code or waiting for the agent to fix it", and that "Replit agents feel more like pair programming". It's one anecdotal Reddit thread.


If you'd rather stay in the loop, our[Replit alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/replit-alternatives) roundup includes Cursor and GitHub Codespaces, which keep you in an editor.


## Checking what an unattended agent ships


An agent working alone for hours makes choices you didn't review, and two papers show where those go wrong. Testing 16 models on 576,000 code samples, Spracklen and colleagues'[USENIX Security 2025 paper](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity25/presentation/spracklen) found that "the average percentage of hallucinated packages is at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models."


That study measured raw model output, not app builders, but builders like these install packages a model picked. The second paper looked at coding agents on real repository tasks. In the latest version of the[SusVibes paper on arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.03262) , accepted at ICML 2026, Zhao and colleagues report: "Although 57% of the solutions from SWE-Agent with Claude 4 Sonnet are functionally correct, only 11.8% are secure."


Neither paper tested an app builder on this list, though SusVibes did test Claude Code, one of the four agents we run. Both point to checks worth running before launch:


- Look up every package in the dependency file on its registry, and remove any you can't find.
- Check who can query each database table.
- Move API keys out of the code and into environment variables.
- Test against production settings, since Emergent keeps preview and production databases separate and unsynced.


Defaults can change under you. Bolt.new's release notes say new database tables have been private by default since October 30, 2026, so a new table in an older Bolt app may need its permissions fixed; existing databases aren't affected. Check permissions in any builder you shortlist, including the rivals in our[Bolt.new alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/bolt-new-alternatives) roundup.


## Getting your app and data out of Emergent


Save to GitHub works on Standard and up. Emergent's docs say "There is no download/archive button", so on Free you copy files out of the VS Code view. The export leaves secrets, database contents and node_modules behind.


Emergent's production database accepts no direct outside connections, so you export it through the Database Manager or support; its database doc says only the preview database can be dumped with mongodump. Moving a published app to your own MongoDB is a "manual runbook", though since September 30, 2026, Pro users get a guided migration to an Atlas M10+ cluster. Plan the move in this order:


1. Save the project to a GitHub repo you own (Standard or above).
2. List every environment variable and secret.
3. Export production data through the Database Manager or support before you cancel.
4. Rebuild, re-add the secrets and import the data.
5. Take the Emergent app offline after the new one runs for a week.


Taking an app offline stops its hosting charge but keeps its databases. Lovable's FAQ says it imports a ZIP from "any other tool", which for Emergent means your step 1 repo, with the data from step 3. If Lovable is the likely destination, remember it's web only, and weigh it against the rivals in our[Lovable alternatives roundup](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/lovable-alternatives) .


## Matching an Emergent alternative to your app


Start from the database, the hardest piece to move later. Lovable, Base44, Bolt.new and Replit host the app and its database on a free plan, though Replit's free app comes down after 30 days unless re-published.


For a native phone app, Anything is built around native output, while Rocket.new, Replit, Blink and Bolt.new (through Expo) also build mobile apps; Lovable stops at the web. If you like Emergent's credit model but want it priced per visit, Blink is the nearest match.


If a developer will hold the accounts and you mainly need a polished front end, v0 deploys into your Vercel project, and our[v0 alternatives guide](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/v0-alternatives) covers builders that bundle more. If the work should keep running on its own cloud computer, with a person you can bring in on an expert plan, that's what we built Awesomic for.


## Running a one-week test


Pick two builders from the table, one that bundles hosting and a database and one billed the way you prefer, build the same core flow on both and compare what each has charged a week after publishing. Base44, Replit, Bolt.new and Lovable can run this on a free plan; for most of the rest, budget a paid month.


If the generated interface holds the app back, a designer on our All-in-One plan, through our[web design service](https://www.awesomic.com/web-design) , can rework it before launch.


## FAQ


### What is Emergent, and how does it charge?


Emergent (emergent.sh) is an AI app builder that plans and builds full-stack apps in React or Next.js on MongoDB. Self-serve plans run from Free's 10 credits to Pro's 750 for $200 a month, and each live app pays 50 to 1,100 credits a month for hosting.


### Can you publish an app on Emergent's free plan?


Not to production. Publishing needs a 50-credit minimum, so Free's 10 credits fall short, though Emergent says "free-tier users may qualify for a free frontend-only published app".


### Which Emergent alternative is cheapest to keep an app live?


Lovable is the clearest case: every plan hosts on a lovable.app address, and its docs say a live site spends no credits by itself. Base44, Bolt.new and Rocket.new also charge no separate hosting fee, though Rocket's database lives in your own Supabase account.


### Which Emergent alternatives build mobile apps?


Anything builds native iOS and Android apps, with App Store submission built in, and Rocket.new outputs Flutter apps and Android APKs. Bolt.new (through Expo), Replit and Blink also build iOS and Android apps, and Lovable is web only. Either way, store publishing needs Apple's $99 yearly developer account and Google's one-time $25 fee.


### What if I only need a simple business website?


Then a full-stack app builder is more than you need. The small-business site builders in our[Durable alternatives roundup](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/durable-alternatives) are built for that job instead.
